item.title: Shafiuzzaman joins Al-Arafah Islami Bank as AMD
item.description:
Prominent Banker Shafiuzzaman has joined Al-Arafah Islami Bank (AIB) PLC as Additional Managing Director (AMD).
Shafiuzzaman brings approximately 31 years of extensive experience in local and multinational banks and financial institutions, with proven expertise in corporate banking, relationship management, investment risk management, investment administration, and recovery operations.
Throughout his career, he has held several senior leadership positions, including approximately 14 years as head of branch, 10 years as head of various divisions, and one and a half years in chief executive officer (CEO) responsibilities, including serving as acting CEO.
He has successfully led several prominent corporate branches in Dhaka and headed key functional divisions, including corporate asset marketing, investment risk management, investment administration, and special asset management.
His professional responsibilities have also encompassed oversight of banking operations and CSR initiatives.
He has played a significant role in driving business growth, strengthening operational efficiency, introducing centralized banking operations, and developing innovative asset and liability products.
Shafiuzzaman began his professional career in 1994 as an executive at the erstwhile United Leasing Company Limited (now United Finance PLC).
During his career, he also served ONE Bank PLC for approximately 14 years and Bank Asia PLC for nearly 10 years, contributing significantly to business development, institutional growth, and operational excellence.
He holds a Master of Business Administration (MBA) degree from the Institute of Business Administration (IBA), University of Dhaka.
With his extensive banking experience, strategic insight, and proven leadership capabilities, Shafiuzzaman is expected to play a pivotal role in strengthening Al-Arafah Islami Bank PLC's business operations, enhancing asset quality, reinforcing corporate governance, and contributing to the Bank's sustainable growth and long-term strategic objectives.

item.title: Inflation eases slightly in October
item.description:
The country's point to point general inflation eased marginally to 8.27% in October, 2026 from 8.34% in September, 2026, as food inflation declined significantly, according to the latest data from Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS).
The point-to-point general inflation rate declined by 0.07 percentage point in October, while food inflation dropped to 6.40% in October from 7.22% in the previous month.
However, non-food inflation increased to 9.89 percent in October from 9.30% in September, indicating continued pressure on household expenditure on essential non-food items and services.
The BBS data showed that food inflation declined by 0.82 percentage point in a month, while non-food inflation increased by 0.59 percentage point.
The overall inflation rate was 8.17% in October last year, meaning inflation remained slightly higher than the level recorded a year ago.
The inflation situation varied slightly between rural and urban areas. In rural areas, overall inflation stood at 8.29% in October, compared to 8.38% in September.
Food inflation declined to 6.37% from 7.18%, while non-food inflation rose to 10.21% from 9.57%.
In urban areas, overall inflation eased to 8.25% in October from 8.26 percent in September.
Food inflation declined to 6.42% in October from 7.25% in September, while non-food inflation increased to 9.48% in October from 8.94% in September.
The BBS data also showed that the 12-month moving average inflation rate stood at 8.66% for November 2025 to October 2026, down from 9.22% during the corresponding period a year earlier.
Meanwhile, the wage rate index increased by 7.63% in October, slightly higher than the 7.90% growth recorded in September.
The BBS calculates the Consumer Price Index based on 383 items covering 749 varieties of goods and services in rural and urban markets.
It collects price information from 154 markets across the country.

item.title: Eight die of dengue in 24 hours, 1,595 hospitalised
item.description:
Eight more people have died of dengue across the country in the 24 hours from 8am Monday to 8am Tuesday, while 1,595 new patients were admitted to hospitals with the mosquito-borne disease.
The Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) disclosed the figures in a notification on Tuesday.
According to the notification, among the new patients, 565 were admitted in Dhaka division, 73 in Mymensingh, 206 in Chittagong, 220 in Khulna, 229 in Rajshahi, 71 in Rangpur, 211 in Barisal and 20 in Sylhet.
Since the beginning of this year, a total of 153,768 people have been hospitalised with dengue across the country.
Of them, 147,158 have been discharged, while 6,136 are currently receiving treatment at hospitals.
The total number of dengue-related deaths this year has reached 474.

item.title: Osmani Udyan reopens after 9yrs: Has Dhaka lost its green refuge?
item.description:
After remaining closed for nearly nine years, Osmani Udyan in the capital has reopened following a Tk147 crore renovation. The park now features new entrances, water bodies, walking paths, recreational facilities and a memorial to the July uprising.
However, the makeover has raised questions about whether Dhaka residents have regained their familiar green retreat or whether much of its natural character has been lost to concrete.
Owned by Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC), the 23-acre park is located between the Bangladesh secretariat and Nagar Bhaban. It has long served as a green refuge amid the traffic and crowds of Gulistan.
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman inaugurated the renovated park and the July memorial on October 19. It opened to the public the following day.
The main entrance, opposite the Police Headquarters, has been rebuilt with two concrete gates shaped like the number 24 to commemorate the 2024 uprising. Inside, visitors will find fountains, water bodies, paved walkways, seating areas and elevated paths. The park has around 3.1km of walking routes.
However, the extensive use of concrete has drawn attention. Former dirt tracks have been replaced with paved paths, while concrete structures have been added around the water bodies.
Eden College student Nadia, who visited with a friend, welcomed the reopening but said the library, food court and health centre should open soon to make the park more lively.
Named after General MA G Osmani, commander-in-chief of the Liberation War, the park was once divided into 11 sections to commemorate the war's 11 sectors. It featured two small lakes, walking paths, sculptures and an auditorium.
Its historic Mughal-era cannon, Bibi Mariam, which had been a major attraction near the entrance, has been relocated beside the renovated Dhaka Gate.
The park earned the name “lungs of Dhaka” partly through a civic movement in the late 1990s, when environmentalists, teachers, writers and citizens protested a plan to build an international conference centre there. Their campaign sought to protect around 11,000 trees, and the plan was eventually scrapped.
Despite later plantation initiatives, many mature trees were felled during development work. Urban planners have also alleged that the renovation did not comply with building regulations, which allow structures to cover a maximum of 5% of a park's area.
The Tk108 crore main redevelopment project included boundary walls, a city museum, a library, 12 shops, a gymnasium, parking facilities, renovated lake banks and walkways. Five new water bodies, a children's play area, indoor games facilities, public toilets and a rainwater storage system were also included.
A 90-foot July memorial has been built over nearly one acre. The bronze structure carries the names of 834 people killed in the 2024 uprising, alongside 20 symbolic tombstones. Relief sculptures depict major events in the country's history, from the Language Movement to the July uprising.
However, the museum, library, gymnasium, parking area and food shops are not yet operational. DSCC says the remaining work may take another two months.
The park has various tree species, including mango, jackfruit, tamarind, banyan, neem and rain tree. But visitors say the loss of mature trees has reduced its greenery.
Old Dhaka businessman Osman Gani, who visited with a friend, said many large trees had been cut down.
“The greenery that once existed is no longer there. It used to feel cool when we came here, but now it feels hot,” he said, adding that newly planted trees would take years to mature.
Another concern is the introduction of a Tk10 entry fee. Abul Hasan, who visited with his wife and three children, questioned the charge, saying the park should remain free for ordinary people, including those who come for morning walks.
The park is open daily from 7am to 6pm.
The redevelopment project was taken up in late 2017, and work began in January 2018 with a 10-month completion target. The original contractor's agreement was cancelled in 2022 over alleged delays and contractual issues. PF Corporation was appointed in September 2023, but the project again missed its deadline.
The initial estimated cost of Tk54-58 crore eventually rose to Tk108 crore for the main project. Another Tk39 crore was spent on the memorial and entrance gates, taking the total to around Tk147 crore.
At the inauguration, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman stressed the need to minimise environmental damage in development projects.
Preserving the remaining trees, expanding greenery, completing unfinished facilities and ensuring public access remain key challenges for DSCC.

item.title: Two injured in Ashulia worker-police clash, 20 factories shut
item.description:
At least two garment workers were injured in a clash with police in Ashulia, Savar, on Tuesday morning as workers took to the streets demanding higher wages.
The clash broke out around 10:30am on the Baipail-Abdullahpur road in the Jamgora area, triggering chases and counter-chases between workers and police.
Police fired tear gas shells and sound grenades to bring the situation under control. Following the unrest, authorities declared holidays at 20 garment factories in the area.
According to police and local sources, most workers joined their respective factories at the scheduled time in the morning. However, workers at several factories stopped working and remained idle.
At one stage, workers blocked the road in Jamgora to press home their demand for higher wages. Tensions escalated when police tried to clear the blockade, leading to clashes and exchanges of brickbats between the two sides.
The injured workers were identified as Alamgir Hossain, 30, a finishing operator, and Razia Begum, 40, a sewing operator at Sterling Styles Limited.
Harun Or Rashid, operations manager of Ashulia Women and Children Hospital, said the two workers were taken to the hospital with injuries suspected to have been caused by rubber bullets.
"Razia Begum's injuries were serious, so she was referred to Dhaka Medical College Hospital. Alamgir received primary treatment and later left the hospital," he said.
However, police denied firing rubber bullets to disperse the protesters.
Mohammad Mominul Islam Bhuiyan, superintendent of police of Ashulia Industrial Police-1, said around noon that police had initially tried to persuade the workers to withdraw their blockade.
"When that failed, we used tear gas shells and sound grenades. No other weapons were used. If any workers were injured, they may have been hit by brickbats. No rubber bullets were fired," he said.
He added that authorities had declared holidays at around 20 factories in Ashulia amid the unrest.
Meanwhile, Khairul Mamun, legal affairs secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Sweaters Workers Trade Union Centre, called for building trust among workers to resolve the ongoing dispute.
He said workers' concerns over wage increases could have been largely addressed if factory owners had promptly submitted their proposals to the wage board.
"Many factory owners are threatening to shut down their factories if workers refuse to work and warning them of possible job losses. The situation can be resolved by creating an atmosphere of trust among workers," he said.

item.title: Dr Khalilur outlines three key priorities for COP31
item.description:
UNGA President and Bangladesh foreign minister Dr Khalilur Rahman has outlined three key priorities for the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, calling for accelerated clean energy transition, predictable climate finance and stronger measures to protect vulnerable communities.
In a video message ahead of the global climate conference, Rahman stressed the need to translate longstanding international climate commitments into concrete action, particularly as climate-vulnerable countries continue to face increasingly severe consequences of global warming.
Highlighting his first priority, the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) President called for the effective implementation of commitments made under the Paris Agreement through faster deployment of clean energy, increased electrification and substantial reductions in greenhouse gas emissions.
He said that more than a decade after the adoption of the landmark climate accord, the international community must move beyond pledges and focus on delivering measurable results.
Identifying climate finance as his second priority, the Bangladesh diplomat emphasised the need to ensure predictable and accessible funding for climate adaptation, resilience-building and addressing loss and damage caused by climate-related disasters.
He underscored the importance of ensuring that financial resources reach countries and communities most vulnerable to climate change, enabling them to strengthen their capacity to withstand its growing impacts.
Rahman identified protecting human lives as his third priority, stressing the need for greater investment in early warning systems, disaster preparedness and community-level protection measures.
Such investments were essential to safeguarding vulnerable populations already experiencing the consequences of extreme weather events and other climate-related hazards, he added.
The UNGA president stressed that international climate action must prioritise practical measures that protect communities while accelerating the global transition towards a low-carbon and climate-resilient future.
The Paris Agreement, adopted in 2015, established a global framework for limiting temperature rise, strengthening climate resilience and mobilising financial support for developing countries.
However, implementation gaps, inadequate climate financing and the growing frequency of climate-related disasters continue to pose major challenges to achieving its objectives.

item.title: Law minister: 24,013 harassment cases withdrawn so far
item.description:
A total of 24,013 cases filed for political reasons and to harass individuals have been withdrawn so far, Law Minister Md Asaduzzaman has told parliament.
He disclosed the information during the question-and-answer session on the second day of the fourth session of the National Parliament, presided over by Speaker Major (retd) Hafiz Uddin Ahmed.
The minister was responding to a written question from Md Keramat Ali, MP for Chapainawabganj-1.
In his question, Keramat Ali said thousands of people were still facing harassment as various allegedly false and politically motivated cases filed during the previous regime remained unresolved. He sought an explanation for the delay in disposing of the cases and asked whether the government had a roadmap for resolving them.
In response, Asaduzzaman said the process of withdrawing politically motivated harassment cases began during the interim government. After taking office, the current government took initiatives to accelerate and streamline the process.
As part of the initiative, a four-member committee headed by the district magistrate was formed in each district on March 5, 2026.
The committees review applications for withdrawal, along with the First Information Report (FIR), charge sheet, where applicable, and the opinion of the public prosecutor.
They assess whether a case was filed to politically harass someone, whether its continuation serves the public interest and whether proceeding with it could compromise the state's interests before making recommendations for withdrawal.
The minister said a six-member central committee, with him as its convener, was formed on March 8 to coordinate the process and review recommendations from the district-level committees.
He added that the government would take necessary steps to withdraw a case once an application was received and the relevant district committee recommended its withdrawal on the grounds that it had been filed for harassment.

item.title: Murder accused escapes from Dhaka court after removing handcuffs
item.description:
An accused in the murder case of garment worker Alo Akter has escaped from a Dhaka court after removing his handcuffs.
The accused, Md Kawsar Mia, fled from the dock of the Dhaka First Additional Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court, presided over by Acting Judge Mosaddeq Minhaj, on Tuesday.
Inspector Mohsin Hossain of the court's prosecution division confirmed the matter.
"Kawsar removed his handcuffs and fled from the dock around 12:40pm," he said.
Constable Arafat, who was responsible for escorting Kawsar to and from the court, said the accused was handcuffed while standing in the dock.
"The accused was handcuffed while standing in the dock. I went to the front of the courtroom to take custody of him, and he took advantage of my absence to remove his handcuffs and flee," he said.
The case is currently at the witness examination stage, with Tuesday scheduled for recording testimony. Kawsar, who had been in jail since his arrest, was brought to court for the hearing.
However, no witnesses appeared before the court. The next date for recording testimony has been set for January 28, court bench assistant Riaz Hossain said.
Alo was stabbed to death in a bathroom at her home in the Dakshin Para area of Dakshinkhan on July 20, 2020.
The following day, her father, Robiul Islam, filed a murder case with Dakshinkhan Police Station against unidentified suspects. Police arrested Kawsar from the Tongi area on the same day while investigating the case. The following day, he gave a confessional statement before a court, admitting to the murder.
In his statement, Kawsar said he had been in a romantic relationship with Alo for about a year. However, she had started avoiding him shortly before the incident. He later learned that she was involved with another man and had been refusing to speak to him.
According to his statement, Kawsar waited outside Alo's house on July 20, 2020. Around 9pm, he saw her to go the bathroom. When she came out and went to fetch a bucket from her room, he stopped her and tried to talk to her.
After Alo refused to speak to him, he stabbed her in the chest and back with a knife, according to his confessional statement.
Following the investigation, Sub-Inspector Sujan Chandra Karmakar of Dakshinkhan Police Station submitted a charge sheet against Kawsar on June 30, 2021.
The court framed charges against him on July 20, 2022, and subsequently began the trial.
So far, two witnesses, Alo's father, Robiul Islam, and her elder sister, Rabbina Akter, have testified in the case. Kawsar had been in custody since his arrest.

item.title: Aminul joins Lahore Qalandars as high-performance advisor
item.description:
Lahore Qalandars have appointed former Bangladesh cricket captain Aminul Islam as an advisor to their High-Performance Centres, with a focus on strengthening player development and grassroots cricket initiatives.
The Pakistan Super League franchise announced the appointment on Tuesday, saying Aminul would provide guidance on the development of its high-performance facilities, coaching methodologies and pathways for young cricketers aspiring to progress to the professional level.
The move is also expected to support Lahore Qalandars' efforts to expand their grassroots cricket activities and strengthen their presence in Bangladesh by leveraging Islam's extensive experience in international cricket and sports administration.
Aminul served as the International Cricket Council's (ICC) Cricket Development Manager for Asia between 2015 and 2025. Before that, he worked as a Cricket Development Officer at the Asian Cricket Council (ACC). He also served as president of the Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB).
A former national captain, Aminul represented Bangladesh in international cricket from 1988 to 2002 and led the country at the 1999 Cricket World Cup.
Lahore Qalandars have established themselves as one of the leading franchises in identifying and nurturing emerging cricketing talent through grassroots initiatives and structured high-performance programmes. Aminul's appointment is expected to bring additional expertise to the franchise's long-term player development ambitions.

item.title: Konate says returning Mbappe in 'good frame of mind' for France
item.description:
France defender Ibrahima Konate said on Monday that Kylian Mbappe was in a good place as he returns to national team action despite missing out on the Ballon d'Or and the controversy in China sparked by his comments about Mao Zedong.
Mbappe, who missed Les Bleus' last three matches through injury, has returned to coach Zinedine Zidane's squad ahead of their Nations League matches with Italy and Turkey this week.
"He's in a very good frame of mind; you can see that from his recent matches -- he's been decisive. He's absolutely vital for us in Madrid," Konate, who also plays with Mbappe at Real Madrid, said.
Mbappe narrowly lost out on the Ballon d'Or to England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane in late October and then had to apologise after a social media storm following a video in which he joked about former Chinese leader Mao.
In a clip from an interview with French show "The Bridge", which has since been taken down, Mbappe had said he was amused by an internet meme showing his face photoshopped onto "some guy, think he's a Chinese dictator", an apparent reference to Mao.
Major Chinese brands subsequently cut ties with the 27-year-old, and Spanish La Liga matches have been pulled from state television broadcaster CCTV.
Konate added that the 2018 World Cup winner had also put any Ballon d'Or disappointment firmly behind him.
"He's a competitor, so of course not winning the Ballon d'Or when he thoroughly deserved it is tough, but the very next day he was giving it his all in training. I hope he'll be in top form next year to lift it," the former Liverpool centre-half said.

item.title: Infantino re-election a 'foregone conclusion', says AFC official
item.description:
Gianni Infantino's re-election as FIFA chief is "a foregone conclusion", Asian Football Confederation vice-president Hashem Haidar told AFP on Monday.
"We fully and publicly support Infantino," Haidar, who is also president of the Lebanese Football Federation, said at an event in Lebanon which Infantino also attended.
Infantino had faced stinging criticism and calls to quit after his plan to sell off commercial interests in the World Cup came to light in July.
With European confederation UEFA and CONCACAF in North America, and initially the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) leading the opposition, it seemed Infantino would have a fight on his hands.
But the Swiss now appears to be in a strong position to secure re-election for a fourth and final term as FIFA president in March after the AFC performed a U-turn and endorsed the 56-year-old last month.
Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association, announced last week he would stand against Infantino, but Haidar said he would not have the necessary support globally.
"Kozo Tashima might get a few votes, but it will be difficult for him to compete, as the FIFA presidency requires maintaining relationships in all regions of the world," Haidar said.

item.title: Sabalenka downs Muchova to win WTA Finals opener
item.description:
Aryna Sabalenka battled past Karolina Muchova in straight sets to make a winning start at the season-ending WTA Finals in Indian Wells on Monday.
Former world number one Sabalenka was forced to dig deep before finally prevailing 7-6 (7/2), 7-5 in just under two hours.
Second-seeded Sabalenka is chasing her first ever WTA Finals victory after suffering defeats in the 2022 and 2025 finals.
The four-time Grand Slam champion from Belarus looked to be in trouble after conceding a break of serve to go 5-4 down in the opening set.
But she broke back immediately for 5-5 and subsequently went on to hold her nerve in the tie-break 7-2 to seize the early initiative.
Both players struggled on serve in the second set, with Sabalenka suffering her fourth break as she served for the match at 5-4 up.
Crucially though, Sabalenka responded to that stumble by breaking back immediately to lead 6-5 and she made no mistake when serving for the match again, wrapping up victory when Czech opponent Muchova netted a backhand.
"I'm just trying to win every match I play, and at the same time trying to stay in the moment and focus on my game on each point and trying to stay calm and in control," Sabalenka said afterward.
In Monday's other group game, WTA Finals debutant Mirra Andreeva motored past Ukraine's Elina Svitolina in straight sets, winning 6-4, 6-0, despite overcoming pre-match tightness.
Third-seed Andreeva, the 19-year-old reigning French Open champion, took control with a break to open up a 4-2 first-set lead and never looked back against her sixth-seeded opponent.
She duly held serve to close out the first set, and then demolished Svitolina in the second set, rattling off three service breaks to wrap up victory.
"I was so tight, I felt I was moving like a turtle," the teenager said afterwards. "I felt like I couldn't really hit the ball so I'm just very happy to get through the match and control my emotions."
Andreeva will face Sabalenka in her second round robin game on Wednesday.
This year's WTA Finals were scheduled to be held in Saudi Arabia but in July were moved to Indian Wells after US military strikes on Iran in February and the subsequent war in the region.

item.title: BFF mourns death of Harunur Rashid
item.description:
The Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) has expressed deep sorrow over the death of its former general secretary and prominent sports organiser Harunur Rashid.
Rashid passed away on Monday night at a Dhaka hospital while undergoing treatment.
He was 77.
He had been suffering from various ailments, including kidney complications, for a long time.
A National Sports Award recipient, Rashid was a former BFF executive committee member, vice-president of the Bangladesh Olympic Association and founding general secretary of Abahani Limited Dhaka.
He is survived by his wife and two daughters, along with many well-wishers.
His first namaz-e-janaza will be held today after Zuhr prayers at the Abahani Limited Dhaka Club premises.
In a condolence message, the BFF president, senior vice-president, vice-presidents, executive committee members, general secretary, standing committee members, officials and employees expressed deep sorrow over his death and extended their heartfelt sympathies to the bereaved family.

item.title: Third New Zealand-India one-day international washed out
item.description:
The third one-day international between New Zealand and India was abandoned on Tuesday without a ball being bowled because of rain in Hamilton.
India lead the five-match series 2-0 heading into the fourth and fifth matches, which take place in Mount Maunganui on Friday and Sunday.
The teams will then play a two-Test series, starting in Wellington next week and Christchurch at the end of the month.
New Zealand and India are marking 100 years of sporting rivalry between the two countries.

item.title: Ensuring safety on roads is necessary
item.description:
Nearly 300 families wiped out in road accidents over six years and ten months is a devastating reflection of the state of road safety in Bangladesh -- figures that represent hundreds of lives lost, children left without parents, parents who have lost their children, and families whose lives have been permanently changed.
According to a recent analysis by the Road Safety Foundation, accidents involving motorcycles, auto-rickshaws, microbuses, private cars, and other vehicles have increasingly resulted in multiple members of the same family being killed together. The findings point to a number of persistent problems, including reckless driving, unfit vehicles, inadequate driver training, and widespread disregard for traffic laws.
These are not new concerns. Yet, despite repeated reports, road accidents continue to claim lives at an alarming rate.
We cannot keep treating these deaths as inevitable consequences of travelling on our roads. Most of the contributing factors are preventable, and that makes the continued loss of life even more unacceptable.
The authorities must take a more comprehensive approach to road safety. Vehicle fitness certification must be strictly enforced, particularly for microbuses and ambulances. Drivers must receive proper training, and those who operate vehicles for excessively long hours without adequate rest must be held accountable. The movement of battery-run rickshaws on highways also requires urgent attention.
At the same time, safer road designs, proper dividers, service roads, and better monitoring are essential. Traffic laws must be enforced consistently, regardless of who is behind the wheel. Public awareness campaigns should also emphasize responsible driving and the importance of quality helmets for both motorcyclists and passengers.
Ultimately, road safety must become a national priority rather than a recurring discussion after every major accident.
Every journey should not carry the possibility of an entire family being lost. The government must act with urgency, strengthen accountability, and ensure that our roads become safer for everyone.

item.title: Who is behind Dhaka's terror?
item.description:
The growing wave of violence across Dhaka, with attacks near police stations, government buildings and university campuses, has created an atmosphere of fear and uncertainty that cannot be allowed to continue. More than 50 crude bomb explosions and at least eight buses set on fire in recent days should be enough to sound the alarm.
What is particularly concerning is how little we know about those responsible. While police have reported arrests and ongoing investigations, the larger questions remain unanswered: Who is organizing these attacks, where the explosives are coming from, who is financing the perpetrators, and what they are hoping to achieve.
These are questions that demand urgent and credible answers, and the government and law enforcement agencies must get to the bottom of this fast. Investigations cannot become an endless cycle of statements about operations and arrests without tangible results. Authorities must identify not only those carrying out the attacks but also the people financing, supplying, and directing them. CCTV footage, intelligence gathering, and coordinated police operations must be used effectively to establish the full network behind this violence.
At the same time, arrests must be based on evidence, not political affiliations or suspicion. Holding the right people accountable is essential, but indiscriminate action will only undermine public confidence in law enforcement.
More importantly, the government must do everything within its power to remove the growing sense of fear and insecurity gripping the country. People should not have to worry about their safety when travelling to work, attending university, or simply going about their daily lives.
Stronger security measures, visible police presence, and timely public communication are imperative to restoring confidence. Violence and intimidation cannot become an accepted part of everyday life.
The public deserves to know who is behind these attacks and what is being done to stop them, and the government must act decisively before this situation deteriorates further.
Restoring public safety must be an immediate priority.

item.title: Dhaka: Miles to go before we sleep
item.description:
Where do you get the best city views from the metro rail? For me, it is certainly the green and watery western side of Uttara. Then comes the stretch from Agargaon to Bijoy Sarani, with the open space of the old airport and the relatively low-density areas around Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University and the National Parliament House. And, of course, the brief but beautiful view of Dhaka University.
What makes these views special? Not just the buildings, but the breathing space between them.
In a well-planned city, you do not simply build buildings. You preserve open land, trees, wetlands, parks and public spaces where people can walk, breathe, meet, play and do absolutely nothing. A city should not demand that every inch of land generate economic returns. But beyond a few remaining green spaces and institutional areas, where is the land available to ordinary citizens for greenery, water bodies, public parks or simply an open stretch of ground?
We are struggling to build more concrete walls, install more air conditioners, consume more energy and emit more carbon. We are replacing natural cooling systems with mechanical ones, then paying the price through electricity bills, heat and pollution. This might sound rude or selfish, but we are literally digging our own grave.
Dhaka has a rich history stretching back centuries, and its muslin was once renowned around the world. Yet look at the city we are building today.
Dhaka ranked 171st out of 173 cities in the Economist Intelligence Unit's 2025 Global Liveability Index, making it the third least liveable city in that assessment. Meanwhile, the World Bank's 2024 environmental analysis reported that air pollution, unsafe water, poor sanitation and hygiene, and lead exposure collectively cause more than 272,000 premature deaths annually in Bangladesh. These are not just statistics; they are a reminder of the price we pay for neglecting our living environment.
The disappearance of canals and wetlands, the endless excavation of roads during the monsoon, the burden of traffic, poor waste management and the deterioration of air quality are leaving a lasting impact on everyone who lives here and takes the next breath.
Living a peaceful life should not be a luxury. Yet in Dhaka, it often feels like a privilege reserved for those who can afford to escape its worst conditions.
After midnight, you might hear loudspeakers from a neighbourhood event. The city never truly sleeps, and its residents rarely stop running. They work to pay rent, school and tuition fees, medical bills, food expenses and transport costs. Even rest becomes something people struggle to afford.
Where are the parks for our children? Where can our elderly people walk safely, during the day or at night? Across much of the city, pavements are inadequate, obstructed or occupied by shops, vendors and parked vehicles. Certain planned neighbourhoods enjoy better walking environments, but access to clean air, safe pavements and green spaces should not depend on one's postcode or income.
The ordinary resident deserves the same dignity.
Dhaka's metro rail offers a glimpse of what is possible when infrastructure connects people. But a city is not just about transport, buildings and roads. It is also about the quality of life between destinations: the trees we walk under, the water bodies we preserve, the parks where children play and the open spaces where communities come together.
And this brings me to a bigger question: Why must so much of Bangladesh's administration, investment, employment, and decision-making remain concentrated in Dhaka?
The government should seriously consider relocating the Secretariat to a suitable site farther out, within a properly planned growth corridor or an expanded Detailed Area Plan (DAP) area. Rather than shifting administrative functions from one congested part of Dhaka to another, we should use this opportunity to rethink how the capital grows.
But relocation must not become another excuse to destroy wetlands, clear green land or build a new administrative island surrounded by congestion. It should be supported by public transport, housing, environmental safeguards and essential services.
More importantly, moving the Secretariat alone will not decentralize Bangladesh. Government agencies, businesses, universities, healthcare facilities and employment opportunities must gradually become more geographically distributed. Other cities need the investment and infrastructure to become attractive places to live and work. People should not have to move to Dhaka simply to access a decent job, quality education or specialised healthcare.
We do not need to choose between development and nature. We need development that understands the value of public space, protects our natural environment and recognizes the limits of a city that keeps absorbing people, capital and opportunities without creating enough room for life.
Dhaka has a history worth protecting and a future worth fighting for. Those green and open stretches visible from the metro should not remain beautiful exceptions in an increasingly concrete city. They should remind us of what we still have and what we must protect.
Bangladesh is too centralized around Dhaka. It is time to expand opportunities beyond the capital, and preserve the remaining breathing.
Arif Hossain is the Executive Director of Farming Future Bangladesh and Regional Head of Asia at WePlanet International. He is a former Visiting Fellow at Cornell University and a Global Fellow at Michigan State University. Email: arif.hossain@weplanet.org

item.title: Bangladesh deserves better than a cycle of crisis
item.description:
There is something deeply unsettling about watching a country with extraordinary potential repeatedly struggle to move beyond the same cycle of confrontation, uncertainty, and disruption.
Bangladesh is a nation built on resilience, sacrifice, and determination. Yet, somewhere along our journey, we seem to have developed an unfortunate tendency to allow disagreements to escalate into crises, crises into national spectacles, and national spectacles into narratives that overshadow everything we have worked so hard to achieve.
And often, the greatest casualty is Bangladesh itself.
Recent disruptions across our industrial areas have once again reminded us how vulnerable our economic progress remains to instability. Behind every factory are thousands of livelihoods, years of investment, international commitments, and the aspirations of people who have worked tirelessly to establish Bangladesh as a major global apparel exporter.
When production stops, the consequences travel far beyond factory gates. They affect supply chains, international commitments, investor confidence, and ultimately the country's reputation.
In today's competitive global economy, perception matters almost as much as performance.
Disagreements are inevitable in any society undergoing political, economic, and social transformation. The challenge is not their existence, but how we respond to them.
Too often, legitimate concerns become entangled with speculation, misinformation, political narratives, and unnecessary exaggeration. Isolated incidents can be presented as national emergencies, while meaningful conversations are lost beneath sensationalism.
This does not mean grievances should be ignored. Workers deserve justice, citizens deserve accountability, and institutions must remain open to criticism.
But there is an important distinction between raising concerns responsibly and amplifying them without considering the consequences.
International partners do not always distinguish between isolated incidents and systemic instability. What reaches them are headlines, images of unrest, and recurring signals of uncertainty.
We must ask ourselves whether we are allowing these narratives to define Bangladesh more prominently than its achievements.
Working closely with Bangladesh's ready-made garment industry has given me the opportunity to witness its achievements alongside its challenges.
I have seen manufacturers investing in sustainability, responsible business practices, environmental performance, and innovation. I have also witnessed the immense pressure businesses face from rising costs, changing international requirements, and global competition.
There is certainly much that needs improvement.
Workers deserve dignity, fair treatment, safe workplaces, and effective grievance mechanisms. Businesses deserve stability, predictable policies, and fair commercial opportunities. International buyers must also acknowledge their responsibilities in supporting the transitions they demand.
These interests are not contradictory. They are interconnected.
An industry cannot prosper sustainably by neglecting its workers. Equally, employment security becomes increasingly difficult when enterprises cannot operate consistently.
Our responsibility is to build an environment where economic competitiveness and social justice reinforce one another.
While we remain occupied with recurring domestic disruptions, the global economy is transforming rapidly.
Artificial intelligence, automation, climate change, supply-chain transparency, and sustainability requirements are redefining competitiveness.
Other countries are investing in technology, education, innovation, and higher-value industries.
Bangladesh must be equally ambitious.
Our national conversations should increasingly focus on productivity, workforce development, export diversification, responsible investment, and institutional strengthening.
We should be debating how to create better jobs, improve industrial efficiency, develop future-ready skills, and strengthen Bangladesh's position in global value chains.
Instead, too much of our collective energy continues to be consumed by managing crises that could often be addressed through timely dialogue and responsible leadership.
The opportunity cost of this distraction is enormous.
I often wonder whether we have begun confusing patriotism with the intensity of our opinions rather than the responsibility of our actions.
Loving one's country does not mean defending every institutional failure. Nor does demanding change justify undermining the achievements of millions.
True patriotism requires acknowledging shortcomings without diminishing progress, demanding accountability without encouraging destruction, and understanding that national development is a shared responsibility.
Our moral and spiritual values teach us justice, restraint, honesty, and accountability. These principles should guide not only our personal lives but also our public discourse.
Justice does not require hostility. Disagreement does not require humiliation. And progress cannot be built upon perpetual distrust.
As a development practitioner, I want Bangladesh to be recognized for innovation, responsible industries, economic resilience, and intellectual capability.
As a citizen, I want institutions that inspire confidence and a society where disagreements are resolved through dialogue.
And as a mother, I want the next generation to inherit a country where opportunities are created rather than repeatedly interrupted by instability.
Bangladesh has already demonstrated what collective determination can accomplish.
Imagine what we could achieve if that same determination were directed toward education, innovation, productivity, and sustainable development.
We have spent decades proving that we can survive adversity.
Perhaps it is time to prove that we can also prevent unnecessary adversity and build prosperity together.
Bangladesh does not need a future without disagreement. It needs a future where disagreement does not repeatedly come at the expense of development.
And that responsibility belongs to all of us.
Sheikh Shuchita Jahan Sneha is a development and industry specialist.

item.title: Explosions heard in Saudi capital Riyadh
item.description:
Multiple explosions were heard in the Saudi capital on Tuesday, as the military coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said it had intercepted a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed group towards Riyadh.
AFP journalists heard the blasts and residents received an alert on their mobile phones instructing them to take shelter due to an “aerial threat.”
“Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh,” the Saudi-led coalition posted on X.
A subsequent message from the country’s civil defense agency said the danger had passed.
The coalition had earlier said air defenses also destroyed a ballistic missile headed towards the southern region overnight.
Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has faced near-daily strikes from the Houthis for weeks, after a truce in their long-running conflict unraveled in July.
On Sunday, the Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh’s business district, where witnesses said the Aramco Tower was damaged.
Saudi authorities said the building suffered minor damage from falling shrapnel after an “attempted attack.”
Images released by Saudi Arabia’s press agency on Tuesday showed the Riyadh region’s deputy governor and other officials inspecting the building, with visible damage to some of its floors.
The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Aramco tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company’s headquarters.
The coalition has in response been launching airstrikes against Houthi positions inside Yemen.
According to Houthi news agency Saba, Saudi warplanes on Tuesday carried out a series of strikes on the capital Sanaa and its outskirts, targeting a gas facility and a building belonging to the Yemeni state oil company.
The coalition initially began fighting the Houthis in March 2015, months after the group seized Sanaa and forced out Yemen’s internationally recognized government.

item.title: French students block dozens of schools
item.description:
French students blocked the entrances to dozens of high schools on Tuesday, the education ministry said, as they kept up protests for better learning conditions.
Student protests across France since September have spiraled into larger cost-of-living demonstrations in recent weeks, some marked by fringe violence and accusations of police brutality.
The unrest comes ahead of elections to replace President Emmanuel Macron next year.
With the European Union’s second-largest economy under pressure to rein in debt, the government has limited scope to appease protesters through additional spending.
Forty-nine of the country’s 3,700 high schools for 15 to 18-year-olds were blockaded on Tuesday morning, the ministry said. Authorities expected several thousand school and university students at a Paris protest on Tuesday afternoon.
“Now is the time to step up the mobilization by continuing to put pressure on the government,” student and teacher unions said in a joint statement released Monday.
Student association leader Ryad Rani said it was essential to keep up the pressure.
“We’re not just fighting for ourselves. We’re fighting for teachers, for their working conditions,” he said.
The government has announced measures including the gradual replacement of an online selection platform to access higher education, as well as financial means for some of the worst-off schools.
But students say this is not enough.
Unions are not happy either, with one leader saying on Monday that a government pledge to increase to the minimum wage by 0.6% on top of a standard adjustment for inflation was “crumbs.”
They have called for a new day of strikes and protest on November 17.
Around 575,000 people demonstrated across the country during cost-of-living strikes and protests last Thursday, according to authorities. Unions put the number at 1.5 million.

item.title: Trump sees 'positive momentum' on Iran after Qatar PM talks
item.description:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday there was momentum toward ending the war with Iran, as he declared that the country "militarily is effectively over," but kept open the possibility of new strikes.
Trump met at the White House with Qatar Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani -- a key mediator in the Iran war. It was his first meeting with a foreign leader since his party's massive losses in the midterm elections.
Trump later posted on Truth Social that the two leaders had "an excellent conversation" and that "much was discussed with respect to the Islamic Republic of Iran."
In the weeks leading up to the midterms, there was widespread speculation that US strikes against Iran would resume soon after.
However, Trump has talked down resuming the conflict while leaving the door open to further strikes -- a position he reiterated Monday at a White House press briefing.
"Iran, militarily, is effectively over. We're just keeping it the status quo," Trump told reporters. "But if we do have to go back in, we are locked and loaded, and ready to go."
In his social post on Monday, Trump said that he believed further strikes were "quite unlikely" given that key US allies in the Gulf "would prefer the status quo."
"We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America's interests are at all times protected," Trump said.
Iranian officials meanwhile expressed defiance at the continued pressure from Washington.
The Islamic republic's top security chief, Mohsen Rezai, wrote on X late Monday that the US "flails like a desperate gambler," telling Washington to "fold your hand. Stop manufacturing fake news about imaginary talks."
Earlier, Tehran's top negotiator Mahammad Bagher Ghalibaf claimed on X that Israel was pushing the US deeper into conflict, adding that "unless Washington drops the 'Israel First' mindset, America and its allies are headed straight for a dark age."
On the ground in Iran, strikes -- which have not been publicly acknowledged by the US military -- are continuing, according to Iranian authorities.
The island of Qeshm, located in the Strait of Hormuz, was targeted overnight from Sunday to Monday, the provincial deputy governor stated on state television.
Trump has acknowledged that the highly unpopular war with Iran was at least partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat, not least because it has contributed to rising prices in the US economy.

item.title: Ishraque: Hasina’s return in December claims political propaganda
item.description:
Former state minister and Dhaka-6 MP Ishraque Hossain has said the process of bringing former prime minister Sheikh Hasina back to Bangladesh through an extradition treaty and an Interpol Red Notice has already begun.
"We seek her return under an extradition treaty. At the same time, the process of bringing her back through an Interpol Red Notice has also been initiated. We want a convicted perpetrator of genocide and murder brought back to face justice in Bangladesh. Anything else you are hearing is nothing more than political manoeuvring or propaganda," he said.
He made the remarks while responding to questions from journalists after a meeting on the law-and-order situation in Dhaka district on Tuesday morning.
Ishraque said Bangladesh, with a population of around 180 million, has only about 200,000 police personnel, excluding members of the Ansar and Village Defence Party (VDP). As a result, law enforcement agencies alone cannot maintain control over every aspect of the situation, making political initiatives necessary alongside their efforts.
"We held parliamentary and party meetings yesterday, where the prime minister issued strict directives. Each of us, as MPs, will organise political resistance in our respective constituencies, working alongside party activists and the general public. We will remain on the streets," he said.
Speaking about the recent law-and-order situation, Ishraque praised law enforcement agencies for their handling of unrest and what he described as attempts to create political instability during recent labour protests.
Regarding the hartal called by the Awami League, he said the programme would have little impact.
"The people of Bangladesh have rejected the Awami League, a party of murderers, autocrats and fascists. The party is effectively banned. Following the 2024 mass uprising and in view of the upcoming trials over genocide, the courts will decide whether the Awami League will be allowed to continue political activities under that name," he said.
Describing the party's recent activities as acts of terrorism, Ishraque alleged that its members operating from abroad were orchestrating sporadic acts of sabotage. He said the activities would bring them no political gains.
Pointing to traffic congestion in the capital on Tuesday morning, he said the general public was not voluntarily observing the hartal.
Ishraque added that the government was making every effort to restore normalcy to the law-and-order situation and address the challenges through political initiatives. He said steps were also being taken to bring those involved in covert attacks and sabotage to justice.
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin Tuku, Dhaka Deputy Commissioner Farida Khanom and others were present at the meeting.

item.title: Your home could be hiding more air pollutants than you realize
item.description:
A home may offer shelter from outdoor pollution, but the air inside is not always free from harmful pollutants. Everyday household activities and materials, including cooking fumes, mosquito coils, cleaning chemicals, substances released from furniture, and mold growing on damp walls, can all contribute to indoor air pollution.
As people spend a significant part of their day indoors, their exposure to these pollutants can be considerable. Therefore, keeping a home clean also means paying attention to indoor air quality.
The kitchen is one of the major sources of indoor air pollution. Cooking with gas stoves can release pollutants such as nitrogen dioxide. In addition, frying food in excessively heated oil can release fine particles into the air. Using wood, coal, or other solid fuels can produce even more smoke.
Without proper ventilation, these pollutants can accumulate indoors. Prolonged exposure to polluted air may increase the risk of respiratory problems.
To reduce these risks, use an exhaust fan while cooking, keep windows open when safe to do so, and ensure adequate ventilation in the kitchen.
Floor cleaners, glass cleaners, air fresheners, and scented sprays are commonly used to keep homes clean. However, these products can release volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into the air.
Exposure to certain chemicals may cause eye and nose irritation, headaches, and breathing difficulties.
To minimize these risks, avoid using more sprays than necessary. Where possible, apply sprays to a cleaning cloth rather than dispersing them directly into the air. Ensure proper ventilation after cleaning and never mix different cleaning products, as this can produce dangerous gases.
Certain chemicals used in sofas, mattresses, carpets, curtains, and foam-based products can gradually enter household dust and indoor air. Researchers are also studying the potential health risks associated with certain flame-retardant chemicals used in these products.
When purchasing new furniture, it is advisable to check the materials and chemicals used in its production.
Regularly wipe furniture with a damp cloth to remove dust. Where possible, use a vacuum cleaner equipped with a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter, which can help reduce household dust.
The cookware used at home also requires attention. If the coating of a non-stick pan becomes scratched or damaged, it is better to replace it. Avoid overheating such cookware as well.
Using wooden or other suitable soft utensils while cooking can help prevent scratches on the coating.
Certain plastic containers may release chemicals into food under specific conditions. Therefore, it is better to use microwave-safe glass or ceramic containers when heating food. Always check whether a plastic container is suitable for heating food before using it.
Mold can grow on walls, ceilings, cupboards, and furniture when they remain damp for extended periods. Exposure to mold may worsen allergy symptoms, cause eye and nose irritation, and increase the risk of respiratory problems.
Such issues are more common in poorly ventilated spaces.
To reduce the risk, remove excess moisture after cooking and bathing. Drying clothes outdoors where possible and controlling indoor humidity are also important.
If mold appears on walls or furniture, simply cleaning the visible surface may not be enough. The source of moisture must also be identified and addressed.
Maintaining healthy indoor air does not always require major changes. A few simple habits can help reduce pollution inside the home:
Keeping a home clean is not just about having spotless floors or neatly arranged furniture. The air inside should also be healthy. Alongside protecting ourselves from outdoor pollution, identifying and addressing indoor pollution sources can play an important role in safeguarding the health of ourselves and our families.

item.title: Can drinking tea lower your risk of heart disease?
item.description:
Many people start their mornings with a cup of tea, often returning to it several times throughout the day. Besides helping people feel refreshed, regular and moderate tea consumption may also benefit heart health.
A new study has found that regular tea drinkers have an 11% lower risk of heart and blood vessel-related diseases compared to those who do not drink tea.
The findings also suggest that tea may help reduce the risk of stroke and blood clots. However, its potential health benefits may depend on the type of tea, its temperature, and the amount consumed.
The study followed 485,934 adults in China over nine years. It found that moderately brewed black tea served warm may be beneficial for heart health.
People who combined tea drinking with healthy habits, such as avoiding smoking and exercising regularly, had the lowest risk of heart disease.
However, the findings also indicated that tea might offer some degree of protection even for smokers.
Jean Copeland, a clinical dietitian at the Heart and Vascular Center of Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center, said tea cannot provide the same level of protection as avoiding smoking. However, it may offer some benefits to smokers.
She noted that the findings provide important insights into the potential health benefits of tea.
Tea is a good source of catechins, a type of flavonoid with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. These compounds may help maintain healthy blood circulation and lower the risk of heart disease.
Some studies have also linked compounds found in tea to a reduced risk of memory decline.
According to dietitian Jean Copeland, steeping tea leaves in water for two to three minutes is enough to release their antioxidants. Leaving tea to steep for longer does not necessarily increase its health benefits. Instead, it may make the tea bitter and negatively affect its catechin content.
The study found a more consistent positive association between black tea consumption and heart health than with green tea.
Previous research has also suggested that unsweetened black and green tea may help lower cholesterol levels and regulate blood pressure.
Grace Derocha, a registered dietitian based in Detroit and a spokesperson for the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, said black tea contains an antioxidant called theaflavin, which may positively influence inflammation and fat metabolism.
However, she cautioned against concluding that black tea is healthier than green tea. Both varieties contain beneficial plant compounds and may support heart health.
Besides the type and strength of tea, its temperature may also affect health.
Several studies have linked drinking excessively hot tea to an increased risk of oesophageal and stomach cancers. Very hot beverages can repeatedly damage the lining of the oesophagus through heat exposure.
The study found some positive associations with heart health among people who drank warm or room-temperature tea. However, this does not mean that drinking six to eight cups daily will provide the same benefits to everyone.
According to cardiologist Anam Wahid, drinking ordinary tea in moderation may be beneficial, but excessively hot tea should be avoided. Drinking more tea does not necessarily mean gaining greater health benefits.
The study participants reported their own tea consumption, and the sizes of their cups varied. As a result, researchers could not establish an exact amount of tea that would provide the greatest heart health benefits.
Dietitian Grace Derocha said drinking more tea does not necessarily offer greater protection. Excessive caffeine intake can also disrupt sleep.
Some previous studies have found positive health associations with drinking two to four cups of tea daily.
What people add to their tea also matters. Adding sugar increases the drink's calorie content, making unsweetened tea a healthier option. Lemon juice, mint leaves, or cinnamon can be used to enhance its flavor instead.
Overall, moderate tea consumption may support heart health. However, it should never be considered a substitute for quitting smoking, exercising regularly, maintaining a balanced diet, or following medical advice.
Those who enjoy tea should avoid drinking it excessively hot and consider their individual caffeine tolerance when deciding how much to consume.

item.title: Chastity, trauma and the subjugation of women
item.description:
Although rape remains one of the most pressing social issues in our country, how extensively has this issue been explored in literature?
Literature reflects human happiness, sorrows, love, frustration, struggle, and the other realities of life, but sexual violence such as rape is often explored less extensively due to social and cultural sensitivities. However, 10,000 Ebang Aro Ekti Dhorshon (2003), a novel by Humayun Azad offers a direct and forthright portrayal of the suffering and social position of rape survivors as well as the stigma and pressure they face.
The novel also explores the underlying causes behind the increasing prevalence of rape in society, presenting these issues openly and without euphemism.
In the story, we see a very young, beautiful, and lively girl, Mayna. One afternoon, a group of perverts attacks and repeatedly rapes her. Mayna’s rejection hurts their ego, so they resort to revenge. Through their conversations, we acknowledge how fearless and arrogant they are about committing such a crime because they hold power within society.
Here, the author somewhat reveals the mindset of the perpetrators, which resonates with Peggy Reeves Sanday’s analysis of rape. Sanday argues that rape is not merely a sexual act; rather, it can function as an instrument of power, control, and the domination of women. As she also states, “Sexual violence is one of the ways in which men remind themselves that they are superior” (The Socio-Cultural Context of Rape: A Cross-Cultural Study, 1981).
When Mayna is found severely wounded, a wail of anguish spreads among the crowd around her: “Who ruined the girl?”
It seems as if the loss of her chastity was a far greater injury than the physical trauma she endured. After regaining some consciousness, she started to thrash about, so they assumed that Mayna may have been possessed by an evil spirit. Her mother seems somewhat relieved by hearing this; it is preferable to her to believe that Mayna has been possessed rather than “ruined” by rape.
As the story unfolds, we see her mother’s apprehension about whether anyone would marry her daughter.
This brings to mind the famous observation of pioneering feminist Mary Wollstonecraft: “It is the eye of man that they have been taught to dread” (A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, 1792).
Her statement shows that society has conditioned women to become more concerned with their acceptability in the eyes of men than with their own personal well-being.
Gradually, Mayna wants to return to normal life and leave everything behind. However, society becomes an obstacle here. Humiliation and condemnation made her life extremely distressing.
Rape is not merely a crime committed against a woman’s body; society’s response can often reproduce the violence and trauma on the survivor.
At the same time, the novel exposes one of the harsh realities of our society; while perpetrators of rape can live fearlessly and unrestrained, the victims have to struggle at every step.
Yet, this reality should have been exactly the opposite; the perpetrator should face condemnation for his crime, while the survivor should receive protection, dignity, and support.
One of the most striking aspects of the novel is how it exposes the ways in which women are pushed into subordinate social positions. In the story, the emergence of a few hypocritical religious preachers gradually undermined the social position of women. Invoking religion, they began devising ways to confine girls to their homes, and many parents stopped sending their daughters to school by their propaganda.
Moreover, these hypocritical religious leaders portray women as objects of contempt, sources of sin, and inferior beings. Such misogynist values gradually seep into society like a slow poison.
As a result, society begins to point its finger at the rape survivor rather than the perpetrator and ultimately, to despise her more than the man who committed the crime.
At a large religious gathering, the Maulana continues his sermon before a huge crowd: “O believing brothers, the world has become filled with sin. At the root of this sin are two chief devils; one of them is the woman... Brothers, do not trust women, just as you would not trust the devil...” The Maulana also says, “Men are the masters of women. Allah has created men far superior to women. Allah created women for men. They were created from the crooked rib of Adam. Had men not needed them, Allah would not have created women. Therefore, women should remain under the authority of men.”
In this way, the hypocritical Maulana continues to demean women in the name of religion, replacing the true teachings of religion with misogynist statements in its name.
However, the ordinary villagers often accept these claims without questioning or critically examining them. Some school-going girls listen to the sermon and are left stunned:
Faju says, “Did you hear that, buddy? Apparently, we are devils?”
Fuli replies, “Who knows how many more insults we have to endure? It seems we were born just to be abused.”
From these brief exchanges, we can understand that a culture of openly spreading misogyny is not new. The girls are agitated, yet they have no power to protest, as if society has decided that being born a woman means living a life marked by humiliation and degradation.
The way religious leaders often compel women to remain subordinate and reinforce the notion of women as the property of men, Judith Butler demonstrates in her influential book “Who’s Afraid of Gender?" Butler argues religious discourse does not merely shape individuals’ understanding of gender; it can also play a role in defining what are considered “natural” roles for men and women, establishing the moral legitimacy of those roles, and ultimately incorporating them into broader political and social structures.
This is evident not only in the literature but also in the society we live in. Even today, a few self-proclaimed religious figures ignore women's dignity in religion and continue to make hateful remarks about women at religious gatherings.
Moreover, with the influence of social media, such misogynistic ideas are spreading rapidly nowadays. For instance, hateful sermons are not limited to religious assemblies; they are recorded and widely spreading on social media. Alarmingly, some social media pages promote patriarchal gender norms and even normalize child marriage.
In the name of religion, they seek to deprive women of their right to education and other rights, confine them within the four walls of their homes, and construct the notions of the “ideal woman” and the “immoral woman.” A woman who is self-sacrificing and obedient, conforms to social norms, and dresses according to socially accepted standards of modesty is portrayed as the “ideal woman.” In contrast, educated, career-oriented, and independent women are portrayed as “selfish.” These narratives help legitimize violence against women. Unfortunately, ordinary people are unwittingly swallowing these toxic ideologies.
Mayna doesn't judge herself by the decadent society's values, nor does she emotionally break down. She asked, Is she really responsible for what happened to her?
Her voice challenges the deep-rooted notion of victim-blaming and compels readers to understand that the victim is not responsible for the crime; rather, the responsibility lies with the perpetrator and the rotten social system that fosters criminal mentality and nurtures criminals. She doesn’t confine herself to shame, humiliation, or inferiority. With the support of her well-wishers, she finds happiness again. One day, she returns to her school, facing rejection but firmly expresses her desire to continue her study.
Here, the author presents Mayna as an exceptional character and offers a lesson in courage and inspiration for ordinary women.
Mayna didn’t demand justice for the wrong done to her. Her silence becomes a protest against a society and justice system that have repeatedly failed women like her. When the village dignitaries approach her to identify the perpetrators and assure her that action will be taken against them.
But Mayna turns them away and asks how many of the other rape survivors in the village have actually received justice. Her question extends beyond her own experience, exposing a larger reality in which seeking justice often brings little hope of receiving it. Through its fictional setting and characters, the story thus offers a powerful critique of the culture of impunity that exists in reality.
Mayna’s experience is not merely a fictional tragedy; it is the mirror of broader social and institutional reality. In Bangladesh, delayed justice and weak enforcement of laws are responsible for emboldening perpetrators to act with impunity and perpetuating violence. According to official data from the High Court, over 35,000 cases of violence had remained pending for more than five years.
In this sense, 10,000, Ebang Aro Ekti Dhorshon is not just a novel but rather a reflection of our society, where injustice persists through institutional failure and social indifference. At the same time, through Mayna’s resilience, the novel offers courage and inspiration to women who face oppression.
Ultimately, the story transforms Mayna’s personal struggle into a broader indictment of a society that fails to ensure justice for its vulnerable members.
Rufaiya Zia Nuha is an M.A. student at the Department of World Religions and Culture, University of Dhaka

item.title: M John Harrison becomes the first science fiction writer to win the Booker Prize
item.description:
British author M John Harrison, 81, has won the 2026 Booker Prize for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything , becoming the oldest recipient in the award’s history and the first science fiction writer to win the prestigious literary honor.
Harrison received the £50,000 prize and trophy at a ceremony held at Old Billingsgate in London on Monday, 9 November. He overtook Margaret Atwood, who was 79 when she jointly won the award in 2019 for The Testaments .
The Booker Prize judging panel unanimously selected The End of Everything after a day of discussions among the six shortlisted novels. Mary Beard, chair of the judges, described it as a book that challenges readers while offering an unexpected sense of optimism.
The novel, published by Serpent’s Tail, is set on the Kent coast a few decades in the future, following an unexplained disaster. It centers on Phillip Tennent and his ageing aunt Marnie as they struggle to survive amid the presence of mysterious, shape-shifting beings known as the iGhetti.
At 198 pages, it was the shortest novel on this year's shortlist and Harrison's first Booker Prize nomination.
Gaby Wood, chief executive of the Booker Prize Foundation, said previous winners had explored science fiction, but Harrison was the first winner to emerge from the established science fiction community. She described the victory as a historic achievement for a writer whose career spans six decades.
Harrison, born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945, began publishing stories in 1965. His previous works include Climbers , which won the Boardman Tasker Prize for Mountain Literature in 1989; Nova Swing , which received the Arthur C Clarke Award in 2007; and The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again , which won the Goldsmiths Prize in 2020.
The 2026 shortlist also included The Disappearers by Marlon James, Black Bag by Luke Kennard, May We Feed the King by Rebecca Perry, The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout and John of John by Douglas Stuart. Each shortlisted author received £2,500.
The win also marks the first Booker Prize victory for Harrison's publisher, Serpent’s Tail, an imprint of Profile Books, following five previous nominations.
The Booker Prize recognizes the best work of long-form fiction written in English and published in the United Kingdom or Ireland.

item.title: grocery store
item.description:
i went to the grocery store today
with a fridge fully stocked.
walked through the aisles with my hands losing grip of the trolley,
fingers slipping off despite the sterile, air-conditioned walls.
like how yours slipped off mine despite our content, contained world.
one that i could pack up in a lunchbox and send away for the day
without fear, as it would always come back.
always be here.
i walked past the plastic-wrapped bouquets of flowers
without instantly pointing to them like a reflex arc;
muscle memory.
poster relationship.
boy meets girl, girl meets boy.
the rest i’ve heard you say a couple hundred times
before we went to bed,
with your eyes lit up, my cheeks flushed red
like i hadn’t lived it all out.
i could’ve picked some up.
it’s not that i can’t get myself flowers.
not like my vase has been filled in quite some time.
but i didn’t. i don’t.
it’s that the smell reminds me of you
and i just can’t quite bring myself
to let that scent linger again.
exactly why i’m wearing this fake, put-together outfit
and not my? your big maroon t-shirt
that i’d wear to run errands.
can’t let that scent linger again.
i stopped by the fruits.
i don’t need any, there’s way too many at home.
i usually slice the pears and sprinkle them with beet lobon,
have them as an afternoon snack.
but you wouldn’t put a fruit near your mouth.
the texture weirds you out.
so i stood there,
grabbing one of each.
apples, oranges, grapes, pineapples.
trying to understand where you came from,
but i’d never get it.
fruits are nature’s candy.
so sweet, how can someone not like them?
but you wouldn’t get that.
walked past the junk food.
now that’s what i probably would end up eating anyway.
that and bhaat and bhorta.
something to sustain me, something to make me happy,
something to have when my missing appetite
decides to show up.
i grabbed a couple of things, paid and left.
walked home safely, but you don’t know that.
i haven’t called you to say that in some time.
i think you’d like to know.
or maybe you wouldn’t.
but i don’t let myself think too much these days,
so i don’t really know.
i unpacked my shopping bag,
immediately put the ice cream in the freezer.
it’s funny how it stood on a cone
when i’m such an advocate for cups.
it’s funnier how i got vanilla when i like chocolate.
you creep up on me, don’t you?
how i wish we could be something more.
something more than a friendship,
but something less than a relationship.
you’re too special for a term
that’s interchangeable with others.
but that’s the best we could do
when neither being together felt right,
nor did being strangers.
i stared at the chips i got.
four of them, electric blue “magic masala”.
i like the green ones.
they were in stock.
but these felt better.
felt closer to you when i got them.
what even is close anymore?
i’ve heard you breathe in your sleep,
heard your heart beat while i lay on your chest.
but now this is what feels closer
than when i counted the moles on your body.
isn’t that something?
i put the last of the groceries away.
the fridge is full.
the freezer is cold.
the flowers are still on the shelf
and the maroon shirt is still at the back of my closet.
i wonder if you went grocery shopping today,
if you picked up the green ones,
if you got chocolate,
if you thought of me at all.
i wonder if i’ll end up forgetting my favourite flavours,
if they’ll change without me realising it.
i wonder if i’ll ever understand where i end
and where you begin.
i wonder if you’ll do the same.

item.description:
Why do I break open before you,
spill salt into your palms,
when I know you will not hold me?
Perhaps for a fleeting moment—
but soon your hands drown,
and I am forced to vanish,
slipping into the dark,
into a dream that gnaws at my ribs,
into a memory so violent in its beauty
that it never truly existed.
